idiom_name: context.Context threaded as the first argument, read back with ctx.Value
implementation_notes: The standard library ships the carrier: context.WithValue(parent, key, value) returns a child context that resolves the nearest binding for a key, and ctx.Value(key) reads it without the intermediate functions knowing the key exists - so the payload is ambient while the carrier is still threaded explicitly. Go's own guidance keeps the two halves apart: pass Context as the first argument and never store it in a struct, and use context values only for request-scoped data that crosses API or process boundaries, not as a substitute for ordinary parameters or fields. For plain dependencies prefer struct fields or narrow interfaces; the context is the right tool only for data that belongs to the request, not to the call.
pitfalls: Keys must be an unexported package-local type: a string or exported key can be shadowed by any other package, and collisions are silent.
Storing a Context in a struct obscures its lifetime and prevents callers from setting per-call deadlines - the official guidance is to pass it as an argument.
ctx.Value returns an untyped value and nil when nothing is bound; without the ok form of the type assertion a missing provider turns into a zero value instead of an error.
